title: The Satavahanas
description: An illustrated map of the Satavahana dynasty of the Deccan, from Simuka and Queen Naganika through the Roman trade, Nahapana and Gautamiputra’s revival, Rudradaman and Amaravati, to the kingdom’s break-up in the early 3rd century CE.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Satavahana Deccan, from about 250 BCE to about 225 CE
note: Based on inscriptions, coins and excavations, Greek writers such as the Periplus and Ptolemy, and the Puranas’ king lists, written down centuries later; each chapter says which it follows. When the dynasty began is disputed, and most dates are approximate and debated. The map is stylised and not to scale; the areas under Powers are painted loosely and are not borders.

west.name: Trade and a rival in the west

steps.title: The Deccan after Ashoka
steps.text: Before the Satavahanas, the Deccan was part of the Maurya Empire. Ashoka’s edicts were carved at Sopara on the western coast, and at Erragudi and Maski further south. After the last Maurya was killed about 185 BCE, the empire’s southern lands slipped away, and new local powers rose in the Deccan.
steps.today: Today: Nala Sopara, near Mumbai, Maharashtra, India.

steps.title: Simuka, the first king
steps.text: The Puranas name Simuka as the first king of the Andhras, the family later called Satavahana, and say he overthrew the last Kanva king of Magadha. They give the line thirty kings and about 460 years, figures most historians doubt. Coins naming Chimuka Satavahana were found at Kotilingala. When Simuka ruled, and where the family began, are debated.
steps.today: Today: Kotilingala, on the Godavari in Jagtial district, Telangana.

steps.title: A queen’s inscription in the pass
steps.text: In a cave at the top of the Naneghat pass, on the trade road from the coast to the plateau, Queen Naganika had her deeds carved. The inscription lists Vedic sacrifices, including two horse sacrifices (ashvamedha), and the fees paid in cows, horses, elephants and coins. Labels name lost statues of Simuka, King Satakarni, Naganika and princes.
steps.today: Today: Naneghat, on the edge of the Western Ghats, Pune district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Kharavela marches west
steps.text: Far to the east, King Kharavela of Kalinga carved his deeds above a cave at Udayagiri. In his second year, it says, disregarding Satakarni, he sent a great army to the west. Where it went, whether it met the Satavahanas, and which Satakarni is meant are all debated. It is the only outside record of this early king.
steps.today: Today: the Hathigumpha inscription, Udayagiri hills, Bhubaneswar, Odisha.

steps.title: A gift at Sanchi
steps.text: At Sanchi, far north of the Deccan, the great stupa gained four carved stone gateways. A short inscription on the southern gateway records it as the gift of Ananda, son of Vasithi, foreman of the artisans of King Siri Satakarni. Which Satakarni is meant is debated, but it shows the dynasty’s reach or influence in central India.
steps.today: Today: the Buddhist monuments at Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The first caves at Ajanta
steps.text: In a horseshoe gorge, Buddhist monks cut the first caves at Ajanta: two prayer halls (chaitya) and monasteries (vihara), now Caves 9, 10, 12 and 13. Faded paintings in Caves 9 and 10 are among the oldest surviving in India. An inscription in Cave 10 names Vasithiputa Katahadi, who gave its front. The famous later caves came under the Vakatakas.
steps.today: Today: the Ajanta caves, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The great hall at Karla
steps.text: At Karla, on the road up from the coast, monks cut the largest rock-cut prayer hall (chaitya) of its age, with a vaulted roof and rows of carved pillars. Its inscriptions name its donors: a merchant of Vaijayanti, monks, nuns, and Greeks (Yavanas) from Dhenukakata. A Kshatrapa noble and a Satavahana king both granted it villages.
steps.today: Today: the Karla caves, near Lonavala, Pune district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Seven hundred verses
steps.text: Tradition names King Hala of Pratishthana as the compiler of the Seven Hundred Verses (Gaha Sattasai), short poems of love and village life in Maharashtri Prakrit. The Puranas list a Hala among the Satavahana kings. The collection as it survives was added to over centuries, but it is the oldest anthology of Prakrit poetry.
steps.today: Today: Paithan, on the Godavari, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: A port under guard
steps.text: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek merchant’s guide, says Kalliena (Kalyan) was a lawful market in the time of “the elder Saraganus”, probably a Satakarni. Since it passed to one Sandanes, it says, the port is blocked, and Greek ships that put in there are taken under guard to Barygaza. The coast was contested.
steps.today: Today: Kalyan, on the Ulhas river, Thane district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Carts to Barygaza
steps.text: The Periplus names two inland markets of the Deccan: Paithana (Paithan) and, ten days east of it, Tagara (Ter). From Paithan came onyx; from Tagara, cotton cloth and muslins. Goods went down to Barygaza, the great port at the mouth of the Narmada, in wagons over long stretches with no roads.
steps.today: Today: Paithan, and Ter in Dharashiv district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Bronzes from Rome
steps.text: Digs at Brahmapuri, by Kolhapur, in 1945 and 1946 found a hoard of bronzes made in the Roman world, among them a statuette of the sea god Poseidon. Roman wine jars (amphorae) and fine pottery have turned up at Deccan sites such as Ter. Indian pepper, cloth and gems paid for Roman gold, wine and metalwork.
steps.today: Today: Kolhapur, Maharashtra; the Poseidon bronze is in the Town Hall Museum.

steps.title: Nahapana, lord of the west
steps.when: late 1st or early 2nd century CE; dates debated
steps.text: A Shaka family, the Kshaharata Kshatrapas, took the north-western Deccan. Its best-known ruler, Nahapana, is named in cave inscriptions at Junnar, Nashik and Karla, dated in his years 41 to 46. His son-in-law Ushavadata recorded lavish gifts to Brahmins and monks. Satavahana kings lost the coast and the passes for a time.
steps.today: Today: Cave 10, given by Nahapana’s son-in-law Ushavadata, Pandavleni caves, Nashik.

steps.title: Gautamiputra strikes back
steps.when: early 2nd century CE, by most estimates
steps.text: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated Nahapana and ended the Kshaharatas. In 1906, a hoard of about 13,000 of Nahapana’s silver coins was found at Jogalthembi, near Nashik; most had been restruck with Gautamiputra’s name. In his eighteenth year, from a victory camp, he granted the monks at Nashik a field once held by Ushavadata.
steps.today: Today: the Pandavleni caves, Nashik, Maharashtra.

steps.title: A mother’s praise
steps.text: Years later, his mother Gautami Balashri gave a cave at Nashik and had her son praised. Her inscription calls him the destroyer of Shakas, Greeks (Yavanas) and Parthians (Pahlavas), who rooted out the Kshaharatas and restored the Satavahanas’ glory, and whose horses drank the water of three oceans. It lists lands from Saurashtra to Vidarbha.
steps.today: Today: Cave 3, Pandavleni caves, Nashik.

steps.title: Two royal seats in Ptolemy
steps.text: Ptolemy, the Greek geographer of Alexandria, lists Baithana (Paithan) as the royal seat of Siroptolemaios, usually read as Siri Pulumavi, Gautamiputra’s son. He lists Ozene (Ujjain) as the royal seat of Tiastanes, usually read as Chashtana, founder of a new line of Kshatrapas. The two powers faced each other across the Narmada.
steps.today: Today: Paithan and Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: Twice defeated
steps.text: At Junagadh, on the rock that carries Ashoka’s edicts, Chashtana’s grandson Rudradaman recorded his repair of the Sudarshana lake, first built under Chandragupta Maurya. In Sanskrit, he boasts that he twice defeated Satakarni, lord of the south (Dakshinapatha), but spared him because they were closely related. Which Satakarni is meant is debated.
steps.today: Today: the Ashokan rock edict and Rudradaman’s inscription, Junagadh, Gujarat.

steps.title: A marriage across the frontier
steps.text: At the Kanheri caves, a damaged inscription records a water cistern given by the queen of Vasishthiputra Satakarni. It says she came from the Kardamaka kings and was the daughter of a great Kshatrapa whose name begins Ru, usually read as Rudradaman. It may explain his closeness to the Satavahanas, though the reading is not certain.
steps.today: Today: the Kanheri caves, Sanjay Gandhi National Park, Mumbai.

steps.title: Coins in two languages
steps.text: Most Satavahana coins were lead, copper or potin, stamped with elephants, lions, horses and ships. Some later kings, among them Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, issued silver coins with their portraits, copying the Kshatrapas. Their legends are in Prakrit on one side and on the other in a southern Dravidian language, often read as an early form of Telugu or Tamil.
steps.today: Today: Satavahana coins are held in museums across India, among them at Hyderabad and Mumbai.

steps.title: The great stupa of Amaravati
steps.text: At Dhanyakataka (Amaravati), on the Krishna river, a stupa begun in Maurya times grew into one of India’s largest, cased in carved limestone. Its finest reliefs date from the Satavahana age, and inscriptions name Vasishthiputra Pulumavi. Damaged by digging for building stone in the 1790s, its slabs are now in Chennai, London and the site museum.
steps.today: Today: Amaravati, Palnadu district, Andhra Pradesh, with a site museum.

steps.title: Portraits of kings
steps.text: At Kanaganahalli, on the Bhima river, excavations from the 1990s uncovered a fallen stupa with carved panels. Some show kings with their names inscribed, including several Satavahana kings and an emperor labelled King Ashoka (Raya Asoko), the only known carving of him with his name. They are rare portraits of the dynasty.
steps.today: Today: Kanaganahalli, near Sannati, Kalaburagi district, Karnataka.

steps.title: Yajna Sri and the ships
steps.text: Gautamiputra Yajna Sri Satakarni was the last strong king of the line. His inscriptions are found from Nashik and Kanheri in the west to the eastern coast, and he seems to have won back western lands. Some of his coins show a two-masted ship. Found along the eastern coast, they suggest trade across the Bay of Bengal.
steps.today: Today: Ghantasala, an ancient port near the Krishna delta, Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh.

steps.title: The kingdom breaks up
steps.text: After Yajna Sri, the Puranas list a few short reigns, and by about 225 the kingdom had split. The Ikshvakus ruled the Krishna valley from Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda), where their queens built Buddhist monasteries. Abhiras held the north-west, Chutus the south-west around Banavasi. In the 1960s a dam flooded the valley; monuments were moved to a hilltop island.
steps.today: Today: Nagarjunakonda, an island in the Nagarjuna Sagar reservoir, Andhra Pradesh.

steps.title: The Shalivahana era
steps.text: The Shaka era, which begins in 78 CE, was probably started by Shaka or Kushan rulers. But in the Deccan it came to be called the Shalivahana era, after a legendary king of Paithan who, tradition says, defeated the Shakas, a story that may echo the Satavahanas. India’s national calendar still counts years in the Shaka era.
steps.today: Today: Paithan, on the Godavari; the Shaka era is part of India’s national calendar.

items.name: Simuka
items.life: 1st century BCE, by most estimates; some say the late 3rd
items.text: The Puranas make Simuka the founder of the Andhra line and the man who ended the Kanvas. His name survives on coins from Kotilingala and as a label at Naneghat, over a lost statue. Almost nothing else is known: even his century is debated, because the Puranas’ reign lengths do not agree.

items.name: Naganika (Nayanika)
items.text: Wife of King Satakarni and daughter of a Maharathi chief, Naganika had the Naneghat inscription carved, probably while she governed for a young son. It records great Vedic sacrifices and lavish fees to priests. It is one of the earliest records of a queen’s own deeds in India.

items.name: Kharavela
items.text: Known almost only from his Hathigumpha inscription, Kharavela was a Jain king who boasted of campaigns west, north and south. His mention of Satakarni is the earliest outside record of the Satavahanas, and it helps date them, though his own dates are debated.

items.name: Hala
items.role: Satavahana king and anthologist, by tradition
items.text: The Puranas list Hala among the Satavahana kings, and tradition makes him the compiler of the Seven Hundred Verses. Later legends tell of his marriage to a Sri Lankan princess. Little about him is certain, but the anthology tied to his name shaped poetry in Prakrit and Sanskrit for centuries.

items.name: Nahapana
items.life: late 1st or early 2nd century CE; dates debated
items.text: A Shaka ruler of the western coast and Deccan, Nahapana is known from silver coins with his portrait and from inscriptions of his officials. His years 41 to 46 may count from the Shaka era of 78 CE, but this is debated. Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated him and restruck his coins.

items.name: Ushavadata (Rishabhadatta)
items.text: Ushavadata’s inscriptions at Nashik and Karla list his gifts: thousands of cows, villages, rest houses, ferries and feasts for Brahmins, and caves and food for monks. He says he went to rescue the Uttamabhadras from their enemies. After Nahapana’s fall, Gautamiputra gave away land he had held.

items.name: Gautamiputra Satakarni
items.life: ruled early 2nd century CE, by most estimates
items.text: Named, like many Satavahana kings, after his mother, Gautamiputra defeated Nahapana and restored his family’s power across the Deccan. His mother’s inscription praises him as the only Brahmin (ekabrahmana) and a protector of the four classes (varna). Some later tradition ties him to the Shalivahana legend.

items.name: Gautami Balashri
items.text: Mother of Gautamiputra and grandmother of Pulumavi, Balashri gave Cave 3 at Nashik to Buddhist monks of the Bhadrayaniya school, though her family followed Vedic rites. Her inscription, from her grandson’s nineteenth year, is the longest praise of a Satavahana king.

items.name: Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
items.text: Son of Gautamiputra, Pulumavi is probably Ptolemy’s Siroptolemaios of Paithan. His inscriptions are found at Nashik, Karla and Amaravati, and he issued portrait coins in two languages. Many historians think the Satavahanas’ centre moved east, to the Krishna valley, in his reign.

items.name: Rudradaman
items.text: Grandson of Chashtana, Rudradaman ruled from Ujjain over Gujarat, Malwa and more. His Junagadh inscription, one of the earliest long inscriptions in Sanskrit, praises his learning, his battles and his repair of the Sudarshana lake without forced labour. He claims two victories over a Satakarni he spared.

items.name: Yajna Sri Satakarni
items.text: Gautamiputra Yajna Sri Satakarni is usually counted the last great Satavahana. The Puranas give him a long reign. His inscriptions and coins, some with ships, reach from the western coast to the Krishna delta. Within a generation of his death, the kingdom had broken into pieces.
